Why gold investors monitor copper

Gold is commonly associated with defensive demand, while copper is closely connected with industrial activity. Comparing their movements can provide macroeconomic context, but the relationship does not predict future returns.

What drives the copper price

Copper prices are driven by a combination of supply-side and demand-side factors that interact in ways that make the metal one of the most closely watched commodity benchmarks in global markets.

On the supply side, the dominant factor is mine production, concentrated in Chile and Peru (together accounting for roughly 40% of global output), with significant production also from the Democratic Republic of Congo, China and the United States. Mine disruptions — strikes, weather events, falling ore grades at aging deposits — can trigger short-term price spikes. Mine-to-metal lead times are long: new copper mines take a decade or more to develop, which means supply responds slowly to price signals.

On the demand side, China is the single most important factor, consuming more than half of global refined copper. China's construction sector, manufacturing activity, grid infrastructure investment and electric vehicle production all feed directly into copper demand. When China's property market weakens, as it has through 2023–2025, copper demand growth slows. When China's government announces large infrastructure stimulus, copper prices often respond immediately.

The energy transition is the key new demand driver for the 2030s. Each electric vehicle uses roughly 60–80 kg of copper versus 20 kg in a gasoline vehicle. Offshore wind turbines require 4–15 tonnes of copper per megawatt of capacity. Grid expansion to accommodate renewables and EV charging requires enormous lengths of copper cable. The International Energy Agency's net-zero scenarios require a near-doubling of annual copper supply by 2040 — a growth rate that analysts widely consider unachievable from known deposits under development.

Copper benchmarks: LME versus COMEX

Copper trades on two major exchanges with slightly different contract specifications. The London Metal Exchange (LME) prices copper in USD per metric tonne for physical delivery, and is the global reference price for most physical trade and long-term supply contracts. COMEX (part of CME Group in the United States) prices copper in USD per pound and is the primary venue for financial hedging and speculative positioning by US-based traders. The GoldAlert copper dashboard uses the COMEX front-month futures close as its reference price, which is the most actively traded copper contract for US-market participants and aligns with the data methodology used for the Gold/Copper ratio.
